questions.text: Show y' = y^2, y(0) = 2 has a unique solution; solve it and give the interval of validity.
questions.originalText: Show y′=y², y(0)=2 has a unique solution; solve it and give the interval of validity.

solution.hint: Check f(t,y)=y^2 and its partial derivative for continuity (Picard's existence-uniqueness conditions), then separate variables.
solution.steps: $f(t,y)=y^2$ and $\partial f/\partial y = 2y$ are both continuous everywhere, so by the fundamental existence-uniqueness theorem, a unique solution exists locally near $(0,2)$. Separating variables: $\dfrac{dy}{y^2}=dt \implies -\dfrac1y = t+C$. Using $y(0)=2$: $-\dfrac12=C$, so $-\dfrac1y = t-\dfrac12 \implies y = \dfrac{1}{\tfrac12-t} = \dfrac{2}{1-2t}$.
solution.finalAnswer: y(t) = 2/(1-2t), valid for t < 1/2 (the solution blows up as t → (1/2)^-, so the interval of validity is (-∞, 1/2).
solution.examReady: Existence/uniqueness from continuity of f and f_y; separate variables to solve explicitly; the interval of validity is determined by where the explicit solution stays finite, not by where the original ODE was defined.
solution.commonMistakes: Stating the interval of validity as “all real t” without checking where the explicit solution actually blows up — a very common error, since the ODE itself looks perfectly well-defined everywhere.
